newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian Met Bureau sees early signs of El Nino.
newsitem.headline: Australian Met Bureau sees early signs of El Nino.

text.p: The latest climate indicators show signs of a developing El Nino event, a precursor of drought in eastern Australia, in the Pacific Ocean, the Australian Bureau of Meteorology said on Friday.
In its latest Rainfall Outlook monthly, the bureau said major indicators include:
- A rapidly falling Southern Oscillation Index (SOI)
- Warming of the central and eastern equatorial Pacific
- Weakening trade winds in the western and central Pacific
- An early finish to the northern Australian monsoon and the development of dry areas in southern Australia in recent months.
The bureau said El Nino events usually last about 12 months and often coincide with drier than normal weather in eastern Australia.
The most recent occurred in 1994 and was associated with widespread drought across eastern and southern Australia, it said.

Much of northern Tasmania, Victoria, New South Wales, South Australia and southern Queensland have already experienced a dry start to the autumn so any further dry weather could have serious consequences, it said.

Although the El Nino pattern across the tropical Pacific Ocean is an important indicator for eastern Australian rainfall, other ocean temperatures around Australia are also important, the bureau said.
Temperatures in the Indian Ocean are warmer than usual, which is favourable for the production of northwest cloud bands, important sources of rain for central and southeastern Australia.
In the medium term, the bureau's seasonal climate outlook for patterns of total rainfall in May to July indicates no significant bias towards drier than normal conditions.
However, the value of the SOI has dropped dramatically in recent months and was minus 16.2 in April, consistent with El Nino type conditions.
If significant negative SOI values are maintained over coming months, the seasonal outlook is likely to produce stronger drought signals, it said.
However, the bureau said an El Nino event is not inevitable.
"The high variability of the climate system at this time of the year means there is a slight chance that the El Nino scenario may not develop," it said.

"However, computer models of ocean temperatures are generally predicting further warming in the critical eastern tropical Pacific region during the next six months so it is increasingly likely that the El Nino pattern will develop," the bureau added.
